We present photometric, astrometric, and spectroscopic observations of USco160611.9-193532 AB, a candidate ultrawide (~1600 AU), low-mass (M_tot~0.4 M_sun) multiple system in the nearby OB association Upper Scorpius. We conclude that both components are young, comoving members of the association; we also present high-resolution observations which show that the primary is itself a close binary system. If the Aab and B components are gravitationally bound, the system would fall into the small class of young multiple systems which have unusually wide separations as compared to field systems of similar mass. However, we demonstrate that physical association can not be assumed purely on probabilistic grounds for any individual candidate system in this separation range. Analysis of the association's two-point correlation function shows that there is a significant probability (25%) that at least one pair of low-mass association members will be separated in projection by <15", so analysis of the wide binary population in Upper Sco will require a systematic search for all wide systems; the detection of another such pair would represent an excess at the 98% confidence level.

USco160611.9-193532 AB is a candidate ultrawide, low-mass multiple system located in the Upper Scorpius OB association, a young stellar region that provides an important environment for studying the formation and early evolution of low-mass stars and multiple systems. The system consists of two widely separated components, designated A and B, whose properties make them of particular interest in the context of multiplicity at young ages and low masses.

Observational evidence indicates that both components are young and share the motion expected for members of Upper Scorpius. Their youth indicators and common kinematics support the interpretation that they are comoving members of the association, rather than unrelated foreground or background objects. However, because Upper Scorpius contains many young stars spread over a large region of sky, comovement and youth alone do not automatically prove that two widely separated objects are gravitationally bound to each other.

High-resolution observations further reveal that the primary component, USco160611.9-193532 A, is itself a close binary. As a result, the candidate system is not simply a wide pair, but potentially a hierarchical multiple system composed of the close pair Aab and the more distant component B. This architecture makes the system especially valuable for understanding how multiple systems form and survive in young associations.

If the close Aab pair and the wide B component are indeed gravitationally bound, USco160611.9-193532 would belong to a rare class of young, unusually wide, low-mass multiple systems. Such systems are uncommon when compared with field systems of similar mass, where very wide separations are less frequently observed, likely because they are fragile and can be disrupted over time by dynamical interactions. The existence of such a system in Upper Scorpius would therefore provide useful constraints on the formation mechanisms and early dynamical evolution of low-mass multiples.

At the same time, the study emphasizes caution in interpreting individual ultrawide candidates. At separations this large, apparent association can arise by chance among members of the same young stellar population. Therefore, physical association cannot be assumed for any single candidate based solely on projected proximity, youth, and broadly similar motion. A systematic search and statistical assessment of wide binary candidates in Upper Scorpius are needed to determine how common such systems truly are and to distinguish genuinely bound multiples from chance alignments within the association.

Photometric, astrometric, spectroscopic, and high-resolution imaging observations were combined to investigate the nature of USco160611.9-193532 AB, a candidate young, ultrawide, low-mass multiple system projected in the direction of the Upper Scorpius association. The goal was to determine whether the two widely separated components form a physically associated system, whether they belong to Upper Scorpius, and whether either component shows evidence of additional multiplicity.

The available photometry and spectroscopy indicate that both components have properties consistent with young, low-mass objects. Their colors, luminosities, and spectral characteristics agree with expectations for members of the Upper Scorpius association rather than older foreground or background field stars. Astrometric measurements further show that the two components share similar proper motions and are consistent with the motion of Upper Scorpius, supporting the interpretation that both objects are young comoving members of the association.

High-resolution observations reveal that the primary component, USco160611.9-193532 A, is itself a close binary. Thus, the system is at least a hierarchical multiple candidate, consisting of a close low-mass pair and a much more widely separated companion candidate. This makes the object particularly interesting in the context of low-mass star and brown dwarf formation, because very wide systems with low total masses are dynamically fragile and can provide constraints on formation and early dynamical evolution in young associations.

However, despite the youth and common motion of the components, the extremely large projected separation means that a physical association cannot be assumed with certainty. In a young, sparse association such as Upper Scorpius, two unrelated members can appear close together on the sky and share similar proper motions simply because they formed in the same broader stellar population. Therefore, a chance alignment of two independent Upper Scorpius members remains a plausible explanation for USco160611.9-193532 AB.

Overall, the observations show that both components are young and consistent with membership in Upper Scorpius, and that the primary is a close binary. Nevertheless, the wide separation of the AB pair leaves open the question of whether the system is gravitationally bound or merely a coincidental alignment of comoving association members. This case illustrates the need for systematic searches and statistical analyses of wide, low-mass pairs in Upper Scorpius in order to determine whether there is truly an excess population of such systems and to understand their origin.

One interesting object connected with this region is often described using component labels such as “Aab.” In astronomy, these labels are used to identify members of multiple-star systems. For example, “A” may refer to the primary star in a system, while “Aa” and “Ab” can indicate two close components within that primary object. The label “Aab” suggests an even more specific subcomponent or companion within a hierarchical stellar system.

Studying systems like those in Upper Scorpius helps scientists understand how common binary and multiple stars are. Since many stars are born in groups and clusters, regions like Upper Scorpius provide valuable clues about stellar birth, early evolution, and the possible formation of planets around young stars. Objects labeled with detailed names such as Aab may seem complex, but they reflect the careful way astronomers map and classify the structure of distant star systems.

## Research Summary: USco160611.9−193532 AB as a Candidate Gravitationally Bound Ultrawide Low-Mass Multiple System

USco160611.9−193532 AB is a candidate ultrawide, low-mass multiple system in the Upper Scorpius association. Its projected separation, low component masses, and apparent consistency with Upper Sco membership make it an important object for studying the formation and survival of fragile wide systems in young stellar environments. If physically bound, the system would contribute to the small but astrophysically significant population of very wide low-mass binaries or multiples, which place strong constraints on star-formation mechanisms, early dynamical evolution, and the disruption of weakly bound systems in associations.

Upper Scorpius is a young, nearby stellar association with a rich population of low-mass stars and brown dwarfs. Because of its youth and proximity, it is an ideal laboratory for identifying wide companions at separations that would be difficult to detect or dynamically interpret in older field populations. Candidate systems such as USco160611.9−193532 AB are typically identified through a combination of sky proximity, photometric consistency with the Upper Sco sequence, and proper-motion agreement. These criteria can strongly suggest a common origin, but they do not by themselves prove that two objects form a gravitationally bound pair.

A key issue is that physical association cannot be inferred for an individual system from probability arguments alone. Statistical estimates may show that the chance of a random alignment is low across a survey or within a given region of parameter space, but such probabilities describe populations, not definitive outcomes for a specific pair. Even a low contamination rate implies that some candidate systems may be false positives, especially in a young association where many stars share similar distances, ages, proper motions, and positions on the color–magnitude diagram. In Upper Sco, unrelated members can appear close together on the sky and have broadly similar kinematics simply because they belong to the same association. Thus, two objects may be co-moving association members without being gravitationally bound to each other.

For USco160611.9−193532 AB, establishing physical association requires evidence beyond projected separation and membership probability. Critical tests include precise parallaxes, proper motions, radial velocities, and, where possible, evidence of consistent orbital motion. Gaia astrometry can greatly improve the assessment for sufficiently bright components, while high-resolution imaging, spectroscopy, and long-baseline astrometric monitoring may be needed for fainter low-mass or substellar components. Agreement in distance and full three-dimensional velocity would strengthen the case for a bound system, although even then the binding energy and local dynamical environment must be considered. At ultrawide separations, the escape velocity is very small, so modest velocity differences can determine whether the pair is gravitationally bound or merely co-moving.

The distinction is scientifically important. If USco160611.9−193532 AB is bound, it would provide evidence that very low-mass systems can form or survive at extremely wide separations in young associations. Such systems challenge simple ejection-based formation scenarios, since weakly bound pairs are easily disrupted. Conversely, if the components are only co-moving but unbound, the system would still be valuable as an example of the spatial and kinematic substructure in Upper Sco, but it should not be used as evidence for the existence or frequency of ultrawide bound low-mass binaries.

For this reason, a systematic survey of wide binaries in Upper Scorpius is needed. A homogeneous survey would allow candidate systems like USco160611.9−193532 AB to be evaluated within a consistent statistical and observational framework. Such a study should combine Gaia astrometry, deep imaging, youth diagnostics, spectroscopy, radial velocities, and probabilistic modeling of the association’s spatial and kinematic structure. It should quantify both the likelihood of gravitational binding and the expected rate of chance alignments among association members. This would help distinguish genuinely bound systems from unbound co-moving pairs and would provide a reliable census of wide multiplicity as a function of mass, separation, and environment.

In summary, USco160611.9−193532 AB is a compelling candidate ultrawide low-mass multiple system in Upper Sco, but its physical association cannot be assumed solely from a low probability of chance alignment. The shared properties expected of Upper Sco members make false associations possible even when statistical arguments appear favorable. Confirming whether the system is gravitationally bound requires precise astrometric and spectroscopic evidence, ideally interpreted in the context of a systematic survey of Upper Sco wide binaries. Such a survey is essential for determining the true frequency, origin, and dynamical survival of ultrawide low-mass systems in young stellar associations.
